name: Matific (Slate Science Pty Ltd)
origin_region: Israel-origin, now Australia-headquartered, global distribution. Founded September 2012 as Slate Science by Shimon Schocken (founding dean of the Efi Arazi School of Computer Science, IDC Herzliya) and Raz Kupferman (former head of the Einstein Institute of Mathematics, Hebrew University of Jerusalem), with Shmulik London, Leon Kamenev and Guy Vardi. R&D and original head office in Israel; commercial headquarters subsequently moved to Sydney, Australia, which is also its strongest market. Company self-reports 70+ countries, 50M+ learners, 50+ languages. Asia-Pacific distribution runs through publisher partnerships including Oxford University Press and Marshall Cavendish. [uncertain] the 50M learner figure is a vendor marketing claim with no independent audit; country/language counts vary between 40-50 languages and 50-70 countries across Matific's own pages.
target_age: Originally and still primarily K-6 (ages ~5-12), which is the SD-relevant band. The task brief describes it as K-9: this is now partially correct - as of 2024 Matific states it 'now offers curriculum-aligned mathematics activities for Grade 7, 8 and 9', so the catalogue is K-9 but the pedagogical centre of gravity, the Adventure Island adaptive game world, and essentially all of its efficacy evidence remain K-6 primary. For an Indonesian SD comparison, treat Matific as a K-6 product with a thin secondary extension.
delivery_mode: online-app. Browser plus iOS/Android apps; sold in two channels - school/district licences (the dominant channel, teacher-assigned) and a direct-to-home parent subscription branded Matific Galaxy / Adventure Island. No offline tutoring, no human tutor component, no hybrid centre model - which distinguishes it sharply from Kumon and Sparks Math in the Indonesian market.
language_localization: Strong on the surface, and Indonesian IS supported. Matific's own multilingual page explicitly lists 'Indonesia - Indonesian' among its supported country/language pairs, alongside Thai (Thailand) and Vietnamese (Vietnam); the Philippines is served in English only and Malay is not listed. So the child-facing UI and activity text can be delivered in Bahasa Indonesia - a genuine advantage over IXL and DreamBox, both of which are English-only for this market. Important caveat: Matific's activities are largely non-verbal, manipulative-driven mini-games with very little text, so 'localization' is doing much less work here than it would in a word-problem-heavy product. [uncertain] whether the parent dashboard, weekly email summaries and help centre are localized to Bahasa Indonesia to the same depth as the child activities - Matific's help centre and parent-facing material surfaced only in English during this research.
pricing_model: freemium trial into subscription, with separate school and home tracks. Home: 7-day free trial, then monthly or annual plans; Matific Galaxy has been sold at approximately USD 19.99/year for a single grade level and USD 39.99/year for the full K-6 program; in Australia the home price is quoted at approximately AUD 89/year per child. School/district licensing is quoted separately and is the main revenue channel. At roughly IDR 300,000-650,000 per year, the home tier is meaningfully cheaper than IXL or DreamBox and is one of the few Western adaptive-math products with a plausible Indonesian middle-class price point. [uncertain] current 2026 list prices; Matific's pricing pages are region-gated and the figures above come from a mix of an Australian tutoring-service review and third-party product reviews rather than a live official price page.
local_curriculum_alignment: Claimed at the country level, unverified for Kurikulum Merdeka specifically. Matific states it 'cover[s] the local curricula of over 50 countries' and demonstrably does deep, code-level mapping in its priority markets - the Australian review notes content 'mapped to specific ACARA codes', and it maps to US Common Core, the English National Curriculum and others. Indonesia appears in the supported country/language list, and there is at least one real Indonesian school deployment (below), but this research found no Matific document, standards-mapping page or press material that names Kurikulum Merdeka, Capaian Pembelajaran, fase A-C, or K13. Treat Indonesian curriculum alignment as asserted-by-inclusion rather than evidenced. Practical read for the gap analysis: Matific offers language localization without demonstrated curriculum localization for Indonesia. [uncertain] - the negative could reflect Matific not publishing its Indonesian mapping rather than not having one.
does_error_type_diagnosis: no. This is the headline verification and it holds up. Matific's adaptive engine is a mastery-and-prerequisite router, not an error classifier. It decides WHICH activity to serve next and at what difficulty; it never decides WHAT KIND of mistake the child made. Three independent lines of evidence converge: (1) the explicit review claim, verified verbatim below; (2) Matific's own engineering description of the engine, which is framed entirely in terms of a skill network, prerequisites and zone of proximal development - with no misconception, error-type or distractor-analysis vocabulary anywhere; (3) the reporting layer, where the finest available label is binary 'Mastered' vs 'Not Mastered' per skill. Nothing in the product distinguishes a misread instruction from a conceptual misunderstanding from an arithmetic slip - exactly the B/K/H distinction this market study is built on.
diagnosis_granularity: topic-mastery-map, backed by an unusually well-built prerequisite graph - but strictly one level above the granularity that matters. Concretely: (a) a skill network of 1000+ interconnected skills with explicit directed prerequisite edges, where 'An arrow from Skill A to Skill B indicates that Skill A is a prerequisite of Skill B'; (b) a 20-minute placement test on first entry to Adventure Island that sets a baseline; (c) a Student Mastery Report that classifies each topic/skill as 'Mastered' (4+ stars, high probability of success) or 'Not Mastered' (0-3 stars, indicating a potential knowledge gap), drillable from topic to sub-topic to underlying skill; (d) spiral learning / spaced revisiting of previously mastered skills. The output vocabulary is uniformly skills, topics, mastery and gaps. This is a better topic-mastery-map than most competitors - the prerequisite graph genuinely lets it walk BACKWARD to find a missing foundation, which is more than pure difficulty-throttling - but it still answers 'which skill is missing' rather than 'which kind of mistake is this child making'. On the field's own scale it sits at topic-mastery-map, not at mcq-distractor-mapped-misconception and nowhere near full-error-type-taxonomy.
diagnosis_input_modality: Interactive manipulative and game-action input, auto-scored - closest to a richer variant of mcq-distractor but WITHOUT distractor-to-misconception mapping. Children drag, sort, partition, place on number lines, and enter numeric answers inside purpose-built mini-games ('episodes'); Matific's pedagogy is explicitly 'learning by doing' with exploration in a playful setting rather than multiple-choice drill. Crucially, none of the following exist: free-response OCR of a photographed worksheet, handwriting-stroke capture, video-explained reasoning, or self-report of strategy. And although the game layer technically observes the child's interaction sequence, Matific's published engine description consumes only the OUTCOME of that sequence - activity completion and mastery demonstration - not its shape. That is the structural reason the engine cannot classify error type: the process signal is generated but discarded. Contrast with DreamBox, which claims to retain and act on the strategy trace.
ai_tutor_diagnosis_reliability: Not applicable in the failure-mode sense, because there is no error-type diagnosis to be unreliable - the honest finding is absence, not error. What Matific does have is an adaptive placement/routing engine whose reliability is validated only indirectly, through downstream achievement studies of the whole platform, never through any ground-truth comparison against expert-labelled misconceptions. Relevant structural weaknesses for this study: (1) the correct-answer trap is fully present - a lucky drag or a guessed numeric entry advances mastery identically to genuine understanding, since only outcomes are scored; (2) the 'Not Mastered' label is a probability-of-failure estimate, so it tells an adult that something is wrong but is silent on what, leaving the diagnostic inference entirely to a teacher or parent who may not have the mathematical-pedagogical training to make it; (3) the remediation move is mechanical - drop to prerequisite skills - which is the right response to a genuine foundational gap and the WRONG response to a reading error or a careless computation slip, yet the engine cannot tell these apart. There is no published validation of the placement test's accuracy, no reported reliability coefficients, and no independent audit of the skill network.
evidence_quote: The task's claim is CONFIRMED, verbatim, from an independent Australian tutoring-service review of primary maths apps: 'The adaptive algorithm adjusts difficulty, but it doesn't diagnose _why_ a child is struggling.' The same review continues: 'A student who can't add fractions might have a place value problem, a multiplication gap, or a conceptual misunderstanding about what fractions represent. Matific treats all errors the same - it just serves easier questions.' Its overall verdict: 'The best of the bunch for Australian curriculum alignment and conceptual visualisation. But it's a practice and reinforcement tool, not a teaching or diagnostic one.' This is corroborated - not contradicted - by Matific's own engine description, which never uses diagnostic vocabulary: 'The principal goal of the engine is to quickly identify a student's zone of proximal development (ZPD) and provide them with activities within that zone', and its remediation rule is purely structural - 'If a student is struggling with a particular skill, we can show students activities associated with its prerequisites.' A teacher review on Common Sense Education independently asked for the missing layer: more 'instructional feedback when kids get problems wrong'.
how_parent_involved: gatekeeper + dashboard-only, with a light assignment power - but never a coached participant. On the home track the parent is the account holder, payer and trial-starter (gatekeeper). The Parent Zone dashboard then gives: learning streak and weekly-goal progress, overall scores and count of completed activities, weekly summaries naming topics covered, and skill-specific performance reports framed as 'strengths and weaknesses'. Matific goes slightly further than most peers by letting the parent ASSIGN activities to target a weak area. But the entire exchange is numeric and topical - streak length, score, topics covered, weak skills - with no narrative of what the child actually got wrong, no explanation of why, and no script for what to say to the child. On the school track, which is Matific's dominant channel, the parent is closer to passive: the teacher assigns, and the parent watches a scoreboard for work they did not set. For the Indonesian parent persona in this study - who may not be able to interpret 'not mastered: partitioning fractions' unaided - a strengths-and-weaknesses skill list is not actionable guidance.
ai_tutor_directly_to_child: no. Matific has no conversational AI tutor and does not explain to the child in language. The child-facing feedback loop is the game itself: an episode reacts to actions, the manipulatives make the mathematical structure visible, and the design intent is that the child infers the concept from doing rather than from being told. Adventure Island adds narrative, character and reward framing around this, and the adaptive engine silently reroutes the child to easier prerequisite activities when they struggle - but nothing ever addresses the child about their specific mistake. This is a deliberate pedagogical stance (constructivist, manipulative-first, low-text, which is also what makes 50-language localization cheap), not an oversight - but it means the explanation layer that an Indonesian SD child on a borrowed phone would need is simply absent, from both the child side and the parent side.
key_finding: The 'does not diagnose why' claim is VERIFIED and, more importantly, is structural rather than incidental - which makes Matific the cleanest benchmark for the gap this study is chasing. Matific has arguably the best-engineered prerequisite skill graph in primary edtech (1000+ skills with explicit directed prerequisite edges, a ZPD-targeting engine, a 20-minute placement test, spiral revisiting), it is genuinely multilingual including Bahasa Indonesia, it is priced within Indonesian reach, and it already has at least one real Indonesian school deployment. And it still cannot say whether a wrong answer was a reading error, a conceptual misconception or a calculation slip - because its engine consumes only outcomes, and its remediation vocabulary has exactly one verb: go back to the prerequisite. That single move is correct for a foundational gap and wrong for the other two error types, which is precisely the failure the B/K/H taxonomy is designed to prevent. Second key finding for the Indonesian question: Matific is NOT absent from Indonesia. Bahasa Indonesia is a natively supported language, Indonesia is one of the four target countries of the Matific Foundation's NIKI initiative (Nigeria, India, Kenya, Indonesia), and in 2025 Mentari Group / Mentari Assessment signed an MoU with Sekolah Yehonala in Batam to deploy Matific Math alongside Cambridge English Qualifications. So the competitive picture is: a credible, localized, affordably-priced incumbent is already entering Indonesian private schools via B2B publisher and assessment partnerships - but it enters as a practice-and-reinforcement tool with a teacher-facing mastery map, leaving both the error-type diagnosis layer and the parent-explanation layer completely open.
study_scale_or_sample: Vendor-collated evidence base, claimed as '25+ peer-reviewed studies across 6 continents'. The specific studies traceable in this research: (1) a SEG Measurement study following nearly 1,500 primary students over a full academic year, reporting that Matific users consistently outperformed non-users; (2) an eight-school Australian primary study reporting an average 34% improvement in test scores after using Matific in class and at home - this is the source of the '30 minutes per week improves test scores by an average of 34%' marketing line, plus a claim that 31% more children expressed interest in maths; (3) a single-school Brazilian evaluation at Escola Municipal Professor Lazaro Sagrado, Colorado, where the proportion of Year 2-5 students failing mathematics or needing special approval to pass fell from 31.8% to 4% after one year (an 87% relative reduction); (4) a University of Western Sydney / engagingmaths research evaluation of Matific (2016). (5) A 2026 partnership report with The Smith Family claiming gains up to 39.9% for Australian students experiencing disadvantage. None of these study the diagnostic layer; all study the platform as a bundle. [uncertain] sample sizes, designs and control conditions for (2), (3) and (5) - these are surfaced through Matific's own validation page and press releases rather than through retrievable peer-reviewed reports, and the 34% and 87% figures are pre/post improvements without a stated matched control.
evidence_strength: For the diagnosis-limitation claim: strong. It rests on an explicit independent verbatim statement, is corroborated by Matific's own engine documentation (which uses only skill/prerequisite/ZPD vocabulary and never misconception or error-type vocabulary), is corroborated again by the reporting layer's binary Mastered/Not-Mastered granularity, and is echoed by an independent teacher review asking for the missing instructional feedback on wrong answers. Four converging sources, including the vendor's own material - this claim can be relied on. For the efficacy claims: weak-to-moderate. The numbers are large and quotable (34%, 87% reduction in failures, 39.9%) but are overwhelmingly vendor-collated pre/post figures without clearly reported matched controls, effect sizes or peer-reviewed write-ups; the SEG Measurement study (n~1,500, full year) is the most substantial and is still vendor-commissioned. Notably, Matific has no ESSA tier rating or What Works Clearinghouse review comparable to IXL's Tier 1 or DreamBox's Tier III - which is a meaningful asymmetry when benchmarking. For the Indonesian market-presence claim: moderate - one documented school MoU reported in Indonesian regional press, plus vendor-side language and foundation-initiative listings.
remediation_efficacy_evidence: No evidence at all that a diagnosis improves outcomes, because Matific produces no diagnosis to test. What exists is platform-level effectiveness evidence - and even that is weaker than the competitor set. There is no RCT, no quasi-experimental study meeting ESSA or WWC standards, and no independent effect-size estimate found for Matific. The strongest available design is the SEG Measurement year-long comparison of ~1,500 users vs non-users; everything else is pre/post or single-school. So Matific can support the claim 'children who use our practice platform improve' at a moderate confidence level, and cannot support 'identifying WHAT is wrong improves remediation' at any level. This matters symmetrically for the gap thesis: the absence of such evidence anywhere in the commercial market is simultaneously the opening (nobody has built it) and the risk (nobody has proven it works), and Matific - with the best prerequisite graph in the category and still no error-type layer - is the strongest single piece of evidence that the omission is a real product gap and not merely a small vendor's shortcoming.
